NOT SCHEDULED FOR ORAL ARGUMENT

              IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
                      FOR THE EIGHTH CIRCUIT



IOWA ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, et al.,

              Petitioners,

       v.
                                                       Case No. 26-3374
U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION
AGENCY, et al.,

              Respondents.




    RESPONDENTS’ OPPOSITION TO PETITIONERS’ MOTION TO
                      SUPPLEMENT

      This Court should deny Petitioners’ Motion to Supplement their Emergency

Motion for Stay (ECF No. 5708597) with additional declarations because those

declarations are proffered for improper reasons in this record-review case.

Petitioners offer these three new declarations to challenge “the accuracy of

scientific claims relied upon by the Army and the Environmental Protection

Agency” and to show “the lack of data” supporting the Permit’s conditions. Mot.

at 2. While declarations may be proffered to speak to standing, irreparable harm,




                                         1
   Appellate Case: 26-3374    Page: 1    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708602
 or balance of the equities,1 they cannot be used to discredit the merits in this case.

The Administrative Procedure Act, which provides the applicable standard of

review, forbids those uses.

       Petitioners challenge EPA’s permit decision pursuant to the Resource

Conservation and Recovery Act (“RCRA”), 42 U.S.C. § 6976. Pet. for Review,

ECF No. 5708024. And Section 6976(b) provides that the APA’s standard of

review applies. 42 U.S.C. § 6976(b) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 706). It is “well

established” that under the APA standard of review, judicial review is “limited to

the administrative record that was before the agency when it made its decision.”

Voyageurs Nat’l Park Ass’n v. Norton, 381 F.3d 759, 766 (8th Cir. 2004); see also

Mueller v. EPA, 993 F.2d 1354, 1356 (8th Cir. 1993) (setting forth extremely

deferential standard of review for reviewing RCRA permits). This means that this

Court’s evaluation of EPA’s permit decision is limited to the administrative record

already in existence, “not some new record made initially in the reviewing court.”

Camp v. Pitts, 411 U.S. 138, 142 (1973); Voyageurs, 381 F.3d at 766; Newton

Cnty. Wildlife Ass’n v. Rogers, 141 F.3d 803, 807-08 (8th Cir. 1998). This

foundational rule of administrative law does not relax simply because Petitioners




1
  See, e.g., Stay Mot., Ex. D (providing declarations to support standing and
irreparable harm); Stay Opp’n, ECF No. 5708599 (providing declarations to
address the balance-of-equities stay factor).

                                           2
    Appellate Case: 26-3374    Page: 2    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708602
 seek interim relief. Their likelihood of success is measured against the same

record on which the merits will be decided.

      Indeed, Petitioners do not dispute the applicable standard of review. See

Stay Mot. at 10, ECF No. 5708039 (stating that the APA standard applies); see

generally Mot. (providing no rationale for why these three new declarations are

permissible under the APA). Petitioners’ assertions that these declarations are

“material” and nonprejudicial because they “corroborate facts and arguments

already before the Court,” Mot. at 2, do not rise to the level of “extraordinary

circumstances” that warrant an exception to this foundational rule, Voyageurs, 381

F.3d at 766. Rather, Petitioners must demonstrate a “strong showing of bad faith

or improper behavior.” Id. They have not attempted to meet their burden to

include extra-record declarations. See generally Mot. (making no such showing).

      Petitioners’ extra-record declarations are also improper because they contain

expert testimony. “When specialists express conflicting views, an agency must

have discretion to rely on the reasonable opinions of its own qualified experts even

if, as an original matter, a court might find contrary views more persuasive.”

Marsh v. Or. Nat. Res. Council, 490 U.S. 360, 378 (1989). On scientific questions

within an agency’s expertise, a court “must generally be at its most deferential,”

Balt. Gas & Elec. Co. v. NRDC, 462 U.S. 87, 103 (1983), and may not substitute

its judgment for the agency’s, Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto.



                                          3
   Appellate Case: 26-3374    Page: 3     Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708602
 Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983); accord Missouri ex rel. Bailey v. U.S. Dep’t of

Interior, 73 F.4th 570, 581 (8th Cir. 2023). Whether delay would worsen the

hazard posed by degraded lead azide is a judgment for the agencies’ explosives and

public health experts. Competing affidavits prepared after EPA’s permit decision

cannot and should not displace it.

      Accordingly, this Court should reject Petitioners’ attempt to include three

new declarations that seek to address the scientific and technical merits of EPA’s

permit decision and to present expert testimony. See Mot. at 2. These

declarations—prepared after EPA’s permit decision—are plainly outside the record

for judicial review.

      The Court should deny the motion.

                  MOTION FOR STAY

      Appellate Case: 26-3374             Page: 2         Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
                                  INTRODUCTION

      Sixty-eight drums of degraded lead azide, a primary explosive used in

detonators, sit in two earth-covered magazines at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant

(the “Facility”). They could explode at any time. The lead azide has been stored in

drums for decades and has recrystallized. It is now so sensitive to temperature,

friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a

significant risk of explosion. And the risk of explosion only increases as winter

weather arrives. To address this imminent and substantial endangerment, EPA

issued an emergency permit authorizing the Army to conduct a controlled detonation

(“the Permit”).    Army munitions safety experts determined that controlled

detonation is the only safe way to treat the waste, because every alternative requires

disturbing material that may explode if disturbed.

      The choice therefore is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is

between a planned detonation (timed for favorable weather, preceded by public

notice, and followed by monitoring and cleanup) and an unplanned explosion that

could come at any moment, with no warning and no safeguards. The United States

recognizes that the controlled detonation will release lead dust. But a controlled

detonation is the only way to minimize the release. The Permit imposes numerous

conditions to mitigate harm, including that the Army detonate only in favorable

weather conditions to reduce dispersion of lead dust, run conservative modeling of



                                          1
   Appellate Case: 26-3374    Page: 3    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 the projected dispersion, provide public notice, monitor, maintain records, and

complete necessary cleanup. An uncontrolled explosion comes with none of these

protections.

      Moreover, a permit is not even necessary for the Army to take emergency

action against an immediate threat from explosive material. See 40 C.F.R. §

270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).   The Army’s qualified explosives emergency specialist has

determined that such a threat exists here. Col. Aaron C. Teller Decl. ¶¶ 8, 30. Even

so, the Permit adds protections the public deserves.

      Petitioners do not challenge EPA’s finding that the lead azide waste poses an

imminent and substantial endangerment. Yet they ask this Court to stay the Permit

so that EPA can revisit alternative options. But the Army already has conducted that

alternatives analysis, and its munitions experts concluded that there is no other safer

option. Petitioners’ proposed delay would leave an explosion hazard in place, with

no end date as Iowa winter arrives. And the additional permit conditions Petitioners

propose ignore the reality that some lead dust is unavoidable. The prevailing

question is whether its release is controlled.

      Petitioners have failed to meet their burden to prove a stay is warranted. They

are not likely to prevail on the merits, and the equities weigh heavily against a stay.

An uncontrolled explosion would inflict greater irreparable harm on the public than




                                           2
   Appellate Case: 26-3374     Page: 4    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 a controlled detonation. Thus, the Court should lift the administrative stay, deny the

stay, and permit the detonation to proceed under the Permit.

                                 BACKGROUND

I.      Legal Background

        RCRA provides for regulation of solid and hazardous waste, from generation

to disposal. See 42 U.S.C. § 6901 et seq.; City of Chicago v. Env’t Def. Fund, 511

U.S. 328, 331-32 (1994). RCRA Subtitle C governs hazardous waste as defined

under RCRA and EPA’s regulations. See 42 U.S.C. §§ 6921-39g; 40 C.F.R. pts.

260-279.

        Hazardous treatment, storage, or disposal (“TSD”) facilities are subject to

regulation under RCRA Subtitle C. See 42 U.S.C. § 6924(a). Owners and operators

of TSD facilities generally must have a RCRA permit to operate. Id. § 6925(a). To

issue a permit, the permitting authority–in this case, EPA–typically follows a notice

and comment process under EPA’s regulations. See 40 C.F.R. pt. 124.

        But EPA’s regulations also authorize EPA to issue emergency permits to

address an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health or the

environment. Id. § 270.61(a). Emergency permits are time limited, specify the

covered waste and manner of treatment, require a public notice upon issuance, and

“incorporate, to the extent possible and not inconsistent with the emergency

situation, all applicable requirements” for RCRA permits and TSD regulations. Id.



                                          3
     Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 5   Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 § 270.61(b). And for the most urgent situations, EPA’s regulations do not require a

permit for

      treatment or containment activities taken during immediate response to
      . . . [a]n immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or
      the environment from the known or suspected presence of military
      munitions, other explosive material, or an explosive device, as
      determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response
      specialist[.]

Id. §270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).

      In issuing a standard RCRA TSD permit, the permitting authority determines

whether the TSD facility complies with RCRA’s TSD regulatory standards. 42

U.S.C. § 6925(c)(1).      RCRA regulations, through permits, impose generally

applicable requirements on all TSD units, like facility standards, preparedness and

prevention, and closure and post-closure care. See 40 C.F.R. pt. 264, subpts. A-H.

There are also unit-specific regulations for particular categories of units, like

containers, landfills, or incinerators. See id. pt 264, subpts. I-X. The unit in this

case is classified as a “miscellaneous unit,” a unit that does not fall into one of the

specified categories. See id. §§ 264.601-.603. Permits for miscellaneous units “are

to contain such terms and provisions as necessary to protect human health and the

environment.” Id. § 264.601.

      In sum, EPA’s regulations scale the process to the danger: standard permits

for routine operations, emergency permits for imminent and substantial

endangerments, and no permit at all for immediate responses to explosive threats.


                                          4
   Appellate Case: 26-3374     Page: 6    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 II.      Factual Background

         The Facility is a military installation in Middletown, Iowa, that loads,

assembles, and packages medium- and large-caliber munitions. See Emergency

Hazardous Waste Management Facility Permit for Storage and Treatment of Lead

Azide, EPA RCRA ID No. IA7213820445 (the “Permit”) at 1, Ex. 1. The Facility

operates under a 2018 RCRA TSD permit. Id. In March 2026, the Army identified

a stockpile of 68 drums in two earth-covered magazines that contained significantly

degraded and unstable lead azide. Emergency Permit Approval Memorandum

(“Approval Memorandum”) at 1, Ex. 2. Lead azide poses an explosion hazard when

it deteriorates. Borman Letter, dated Aug. 12, 2026 (“First Army Letter”), Ex. 3.

Those risks increase in cold weather because the lead azide crystalizes, which

increases the sensitivity of the lead azide—leading to an increased risk of an

unintended explosion. Approval Memorandum at 2. In this condition, disruption

like friction or movement poses an unacceptable risk of an uncontrolled explosion.

Id.; First Army Letter. The drums cannot even be opened. Crystal growth inside the

barrels and around the lids makes the lids unsafe to remove, so the water-ethanol

solution that keeps the material stable has not been checked or replenished since

September 2025, and evaporation has left it more prone to freezing. Teller Decl. ¶¶

11–13.




                                          5
      Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 7   Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
        EPA confirmed the lead azide stockpile as hazardous waste because of both

its reactivity (tendency to explode) and its lead toxicity. Permit at 2. After

determining that the location of the lead waste was not authorized for treatment,

storage, or disposal under the 2018 permit, the Army applied for three successive

emergency permits to continue storing the lead azide waste while it determined an

appropriate treatment for it. Id.

       In September 2026, the Army submitted a permit application proposing to

treat the lead azide waste by a controlled detonation. Id. at 3. The Army’s

recommended course was based on an analysis of a range of treatment options. Id.

at 2; First Army Letter. Army explosives safety experts determined that controlled

detonation was the only safe option given the unstable condition of the waste.

Borman Letter, dated Sep. 4, 2026 (“Second Army Letter”), Ex. 4. The Army

concluded that open detonation (a kind of treatment under RCRA) of this waste at

Army’s already permitted Open Burn/Open Detonation Unit would involve moving

the unstable lead azide and posed an unacceptable risk of an uncontrolled explosion.

Id. at 2.

       On November 13, 2026, EPA approved the Army’s emergency permit

application and issued the Permit based on three critical findings. First, EPA found

that the lead azide waste posed an imminent and substantial endangerment because

of the risk of an uncontrolled explosion. Permit at 1. Second, EPA credited the



                                         6
   Appellate Case: 26-3374     Page: 8   Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 Army explosives experts’ assessment and treatment alternatives analysis, which

found no safe treatment option other than detonation. Approval Memorandum at 3.

EPA therefore found that treatment by controlled detonation was necessary to

protect human health and the environment from the greater risk of an uncontrolled

explosion. Id. at 2-3. Third, EPA found that a controlled detonation would allow

the Army to time the operation to favorable weather conditions, reducing blast-

debris dispersal, while also providing advance public notice and facilitating safe

evacuation of nearby areas. Id. at 2-6.

      EPA included numerous permit conditions to minimize the risks to human

health and the environment, including maintenance of blast containment barriers,

public notice requirements, weather restrictions that allow detonation only when

dispersal of lead dust would be limited and directed away from large population

centers, and lead dust remediation requirements over the area of possible dispersal.

Approval Memorandum at 4-6; see also Permit §§ IV.D, IV.F–G, IV.O.3, IV.U–X,

app. C. EPA required very conservative air modelling that assumes 100 percent of

the lead waste would become airborne without considering that mitigation measures.

Permit at 3, app. B, ¶ A. EPA also included conditions to minimize exposure from

all potential sources (e.g., soil, air, etc.). Id. §§ IV.Q.1.i, IV.U.1, IV.V, app. C.

      For notice, the Permit requires the Army to publicly distribute a preliminary

air dispersion estimate at least five days before treatment, update it at least 48 hours



                                            7
   Appellate Case: 26-3374      Page: 9    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 before treatment, and begin hourly updates six hours before detonation. Id. §§

IV.G.1.i–ii. The Army also must provide notices to explain the geographic extent

and expected duration of potential exposure and to identify protective actions for

residents and workers in areas of modeled deposition. Id., app. C ¶¶ B.1.ii.e–f, B.2.i–

ii.

         The Permit also requires specific cleaning and dust-mitigation instructions for

areas where projected surface deposition exceeds 100 micrograms per square foot.

Id., app. C, ¶ B.2.ii.b. The Permit separately requires monitoring at the facility and

off site, a final air dispersion estimate within six hours after detonation, and

corrective action (i.e., clean up) on and beyond the facility as necessary to protect

human health and the environment. Id. §§ IV.Q.1.i, IV.G.1.iii, and at 3. Within 24

hours after treatment, the Army must initiate soil and high-touch-surface sampling

at covered locations in the higher-deposition area where it has permission to enter.

Id. § IV.U.2.ii.

         On November 15, 2026, the Army issued a public advisory announcing that

treatment was planned for November 20, 2026.1 On November 19, 2026, Petitioners

filed a petition for review and an emergency motion to stay the Permit. The Army

                                            8
      Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 10    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 then delayed the planned detonation to November 23, 2026. 2 Also on November 19,

2026, this Court administratively stayed the Permit until the Court rules on

Petitioners’ motion. The Army postponed the planned detonation to November 23,

2026, and then to November 24. 3 See Notice, Dkt. No. 5708596.

                                    ARGUMENT

I.      Even if the Court stays the Permit, the Army is not precluded from
        taking requisite emergency action.

        There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Facility will

spontaneously explode. Teller Decl. The waste has deteriorated to a degree that it

is extremely sensitive to friction from crystal formation. Id. ¶ 9. The barrels holding

the waste cannot be removed due to the risk of explosion, preventing the Army from

taking measures to reduce the risk of explosion. Id. ¶¶ 12-13. As the temperatures

drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can

break more easily in freezing temperatures. Id. ¶ 13. If the crystals break, this could

cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead

azide into the environment. Id. ¶¶ 15, 17. Temperatures have already dropped below

30 degrees Fahrenheit, with temperature swings as low as 24 degrees and high as 70




2
  Army, Postponed: Lead Azide Detonation (Nov. 19, 2026),
https://www.army.mil/article/296926 [https://perma.cc/WBS3-69HG].
3
  Army, Postponed: Lead Azide Detonation (Nov. 19, 2026),
https://www.army.mil/article/296926 [https://perma.cc/WBS3-69HG].

                                          9
     Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 11    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 degrees. Id. ¶¶ 28-29. These temperature swings have dramatically increased the

risk of an uncontrolled explosion and threat to public safety. Id. ¶ 29.

      Under these circumstances, EPA’s RCRA regulations provide an exemption

from both substantive and permitting requirements to allow immediate action. The

RCRA regulations provide that the substantive standards “do not apply to”:

      a person engaged in treatment or containment activities during
      immediate response to . . . [a]n immediate threat to human health,
      public safety, property, or the environment, from the known or
      suspected presence of military munitions, other explosive material, or
      an explosive device, as determined by an explosive or munitions
      emergency response specialist as defined in 40 [C.F.R.] § 260.10.

40 C.F.R. § 264.1(g)(8)(i)(D). The same exclusion from permitting requirements is

at 40 C.F.R. § 270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).

      Here, an explosive or munitions emergency specialist has made the requisite

determination. Teller Decl. ¶ 3. Thus, EPA’s RCRA regulations allow the Army to

conduct a controlled detonation of the lead azide at the Facility even if the Permit

that is at issue here is not in effect. Any other options require handling the lead azide

in a way that poses an unacceptable risk of an uncontrolled explosion. See id. ¶¶ 6-

17. A controlled detonation would minimize the risk associated with the resulting

explosion. See id. ¶¶ 16-25. Thus, a controlled detonation is necessary now to

respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion at the Facility. EPA’s

regulations allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit, and the

Army intends to act on November 24, 2026.


                                           10
  Appellate Case: 26-3374      Page: 12     Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 II.      The Court should lift the administrative stay and deny Petitioners’
         stay motion.

         A stay, like a preliminary injunction, “is an extraordinary and drastic remedy,”

and Petitioners have not made a “a clear showing” that one should be granted.

Mazurek v. Armstrong, 520 U.S. 968, 972 (1997). They must demonstrate: (1) a

likelihood of success on the merits; (2) irreparable injury if relief is withheld; (3)

lack of harm to other parties from a stay; and (4) that a stay would serve the public

interest. Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 434 (2009). The third and fourth criteria

merge here. Id. at 435. A stay is not a matter of right, even if irreparable injury

might otherwise result.” Id. at 433. Rather, courts “pay particular regard for the

public consequences in employing the extraordinary remedy.”              Weinberger v.

Romero-Barcelo, 456 U.S. 305, 312 (1982). Accordingly, courts “must balance the

competing claims of injury and must consider the effect on each party of the granting

or withholding of the requested relief.” Winter v. NRDC, 555 U.S. 7, 24, (2008).

         Petitioners have not made the requisite “clear showing,” Mazurek, 520 U.S.

at 972, that they are “likely” to prevail on the merits. Starbucks Corp. v. McKinney,

602 U.S. 339, 349 (2024) (citation modified). EPA issued the Permit because the

unstable lead azide at the Facility poses an imminent and substantial endangerment.

Petitioners do not challenge that determination. Instead, they ask this Court to

second-guess the agencies’ technical judgments about the specific permit terms

needed to protect human health and the environment during a controlled detonation.


                                            11
      Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 13     Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 The decision to authorize treatment by a controlled detonation was reasonable, and

so were the permit terms to minimize risk. And the equities strongly favor a

controlled, planned detonation over the imminent, uncontrolled one that the stay

invites. Petitioners cannot show that the public will not be harmed if the Permit is

stayed. The Court should deny the motion.

      A.     Petitioners are unlikely to prevail on the merits.

      RCRA imposes a high bar to reverse EPA permitting decisions under the

Administrative Procedure Act standard of review. See, e.g., Mueller v. EPA, 993

F.2d 1354, 1356 (8th Cir. 1993); Greenpeace, Inc. v. Waste Techs. Indus., 9 F.3d

1174, 1180 (6th Cir. 1993). And Petitioners’ burden is even higher when an

agency’s decisions rest on highly technical judgments. See Missouri ex rel. Bailey

v. U.S. Dep’t of Interior, 73 F.4th 570, 581 (8th Cir. 2023). Plaintiffs have not made

a clear showing they are likely to succeed.

             1.    EPA reasonably authorized a controlled detonation to
                   avert a more damaging uncontrolled explosion.

      EPA reasonably determined that controlled detonation of the lead azide waste

was necessary based on the imminent and substantial endangerment at the Facility.

The crystallized, deteriorated lead azide waste is unstable and can explode

spontaneously. Approval Memorandum at 2; First Army Letter. Army explosive

experts evaluated the waste and determined that a mitigated, controlled detonation

is the only safe treatment option. Approval Letter at 3; First Army Letter. In doing


                                         12
  Appellate Case: 26-3374     Page: 14    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 so, the Army considered “the full range of potential alternative for the treatment of

the lead azide,” including in place treatment, thermal treatment, relocation of drums,

and controlled detonation. Second Army Letter. The Army’s technical consensus

was that controlled detonation is the only safe option. Id. Other options that would

disturb the containers, like in-place chemical neutralization, would create an

unacceptable risk of an unintentional detonation. First Army Letter. And as the

weather gets colder, the risk of unintentional detonation increases as crystal

formation increases. Approval Memorandum at 2; First Army Letter.

      EPA’s determination that the controlled detonation was necessary to protect

human health and the environment was reasonable because it is more protective than

allowing the waste to unintentionally explode. In a controlled explosion, the Army

accounts for weather conditions that limit the spread of lead dust.         Approval

Memorandum at 5-6. For example, the Army can detonate on a day when the wind

is blowing away from population centers and at lower speeds that will reduce the

geographic extent of lead dispersion. Id. Further, during a controlled detonation,

the Army can ensure complete treatment of the waste. As EPA explained, “[t]he

possibility of spontaneous detonation may result in greater harm to human health

because the conditions of detonation would not be controlled to mitigate its impact.”

Approval Memorandum at 3. It was reasonable for EPA to give weight to the

Army’s munitions experts. And that is especially true where qualifying Army



                                         13
  Appellate Case: 26-3374     Page: 15    Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 munitions experts are empowered to take immediate action based on immediate

threats even without a permit. See 40 C.F.R. § 270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).

      Petitioners theorize that treatment alternatives other than controlled

detonation, like chemical neutralization, may be feasible at the Facility. Mot. 18-

22. But the Army’s munitions experts considered those options and determined that

they are not safe and pose an unacceptable risk of an unintentional explosion.

Second Army Letter. Petitioners ignore the critical finding that even disturbing the

containers poses an unacceptable risk because friction from any movement can set

off an explosion. First Army Letter; Second Army Letter. EPA’s and the Army’s

determination that a controlled detonation is necessary to protect human health and

the environment is a highly technical judgment that warrants deference.         See

Missouri ex rel. Bailey, 73 F.4th at 581. The Court should not displace those expert

judgments with Petitioners’ unsubstantiated hope that a safer method might exist.

            2.     EPA reasonably crafted the Permit to include
                   necessary terms and conditions to protect human
                   health and the environment.

                                  INTRODUCTION

      Sixty-eight drums of degraded lead azide, a primary explosive used in

detonators, sit in two earth-covered magazines at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant

(the “Facility”). They could explode at any time. The lead azide has been stored in

drums for decades and has recrystallized. It is now so sensitive to temperature,

friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a

significant risk of explosion. And the risk of explosion only increases as winter

weather arrives. To address this imminent and substantial endangerment, EPA

issued an emergency permit authorizing the Army to conduct a controlled detonation

(“the Permit”).    Army munitions safety experts determined that controlled

detonation is the only safe way to treat the waste, because every alternative requires

disturbing material that may explode if disturbed.

      The choice therefore is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is

between a planned detonation (timed for favorable weather, preceded by public

notice, and followed by monitoring and cleanup) and an unplanned explosion that

could come at any moment, with no warning and no safeguards. The United States

recognizes that the controlled detonation will release lead dust. But a controlled

detonation is the only way to minimize the release. The Permit imposes numerous

conditions to mitigate harm, including that the Army detonate only in favorable

weather conditions to reduce dispersion of lead dust, run conservative modeling of

 the projected dispersion, provide public notice, monitor, maintain records, and

complete necessary cleanup. An uncontrolled explosion comes with none of these

protections.

      Moreover, a permit is not even necessary for the Army to take emergency

action against an immediate threat from explosive material. See 40 C.F.R. §

270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).   The Army’s qualified explosives emergency specialist has

determined that such a threat exists here. Col. Aaron C. Teller Decl. ¶¶ 8, 30. Even

so, the Permit adds protections the public deserves.

      Petitioners do not challenge EPA’s finding that the lead azide waste poses an

imminent and substantial endangerment. Yet they ask this Court to stay the Permit

so that EPA can revisit alternative options. But the Army already has conducted that

alternatives analysis, and its munitions experts concluded that there is no other safer

option. Petitioners’ proposed delay would leave an explosion hazard in place, with

no end date as Iowa winter arrives. And the additional permit conditions Petitioners

propose ignore the reality that some lead dust is unavoidable. The prevailing

question is whether its release is controlled.

      Petitioners have failed to meet their burden to prove a stay is warranted. They

are not likely to prevail on the merits, and the equities weigh heavily against a stay.

I.      Legal Background

        RCRA provides for regulation of solid and hazardous waste, from generation

to disposal. See 42 U.S.C. § 6901 et seq.; City of Chicago v. Env’t Def. Fund, 511

U.S. 328, 331-32 (1994). RCRA Subtitle C governs hazardous waste as defined

under RCRA and EPA’s regulations. See 42 U.S.C. §§ 6921-39g; 40 C.F.R. pts.

260-279.

        Hazardous treatment, storage, or disposal (“TSD”) facilities are subject to

regulation under RCRA Subtitle C. See 42 U.S.C. § 6924(a). Owners and operators

of TSD facilities generally must have a RCRA permit to operate. Id. § 6925(a). To

issue a permit, the permitting authority–in this case, EPA–typically follows a notice

and comment process under EPA’s regulations. See 40 C.F.R. pt. 124.

        But EPA’s regulations also authorize EPA to issue emergency permits to

address an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health or the

environment. Id. § 270.61(a). Emergency permits are time limited, specify the

covered waste and manner of treatment, require a public notice upon issuance, and

“incorporate, to the extent possible and not inconsistent with the emergency

situation, all applicable requirements” for RCRA permits and TSD regulations. Id.



                                          3
     Appellate Case: 26-3374   Page: 5   Date Filed: 11/22/2026 Entry ID: 5708599
 § 270.61(b). And for the most urgent situations, EPA’s regulations do not require a

permit for

      treatment or containment activities taken during immediate response to
      . . . [a]n immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or
      the environment from the known or suspected presence of military
      munitions, other explosive material, or an explosive device, as
      determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response
      specialist[.]

Id. §270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).

      In issuing a standard RCRA TSD permit, the permitting authority determines

whether the TSD facility complies with RCRA’s TSD regulatory standards. 42

U.S.C. § 6925(c)(1).      RCRA regulations, through permits, impose generally

applicable requirements on all TSD units, like facility standards, preparedness and

prevention, and closure and post-closure care. See 40 C.F.R. pt. 264, subpts. A-H.

There are also unit-specific regulations for particular categories of units, like

containers, landfills, or incinerators. See id. pt 264, subpts. I-X. The unit in this

case is classified as a “miscellaneous unit,” a unit that does not fall into one of the

specified categories. See id. §§ 264.601-.603. Permits for miscellaneous units “are

to contain such terms and provisions as necessary to protect human health and the

environment.” Id. § 264.601.

      In sum, EPA’s regulations scale the process to the danger: standard permits

for routine operations, emergency permits for imminent and substantial

endangerments, and no permit at all for immediate responses to explosive threats.

Optimizing Protectiveness of the Emergency Permit

        25.     The timeliness of EPA’s emergency permit—and the Army’s readiness to

implement the activity that it authorizes—is critical to the protection of human health and the

environment. To make the permit optimally protective, EPA’s permitting decision had to balance

competing risk factors. On one hand, the permit had to impose requirements that mitigate the

environmental impact and human health risks that will inevitably result from the treatment

activity. On the other hand, the permit could not be so constraining that the Army would be

unable to complete the treatment activity before winter conditions increase the chance of

spontaneous explosion.

        26.     In light of these challenging circumstances, EPA’s emergency permit requires the

Army to take concrete actions before, during, and after the detonation to enhance protection of

human health and the environment. The requirements take the form of special permit conditions

that are designed to mitigate the exposures, to the extent feasible, and to remediate the

contamination that EPA expects will result from the detonation. Broadly speaking, these risks are

presented both on the IAAAP installation itself and, more critically, in the off-site areas that will

be affected by airborne lead migration and deposition.

        27.     After careful review of the Army’s permit application, my staff informed me that

off-site risk to human health arises from two potential pathways of exposure to lead. The first

exposure pathway is from inhalation, dermal contact, and incidental ingestion of lead suspended

as a particulate in ambient air. In addition, the airborne transport of lead is expected to result in

the deposition of lead particles at varying concentrations across the path of dispersion. Air

indicated that dust-lead deposition is expected to occur at higher concentrations closer to the

detonation site and to decrease with distance from IAAAP.

       28.     To address the air and dust exposure pathways, an essential requirement of the

emergency permit is timely public notification of expected exposure risk in areas where air

dispersion modeling predicts potential airborne lead migration and dust deposition. To

implement such notifications, my staff developed special permit conditions that require the Army

to iteratively model projected airborne migration and dust-lead deposition areas. With each

iteration, the Army is required to publicly distribute updated imagery of the potential impact area

and to provide members of the public with information about protective actions that should be

taken within those areas. In practice, implementation of this public notification requirement

allows people within affected areas to make informed decisions that minimize their exposure to

lead. To maximize such precautionary measures, the permit requires the Army’s modeling to

utilize conservative parameters that ensure the modeling outputs do not under-predict the extent

of potential impact. Specifically, the required modeling assumes that 100 percent of lead content

in the lead azide waste will be released to the ambient air, an assumption that both Army and

EPA technical teams agree is not realistic but nevertheless necessary for maximal public

awareness of potential risk.

       29.     In addition to public notification, the Emergency Permit aims to mitigate off-site

exposures by defining adverse meteorological conditions during which the detonation must not

occur. As indicated in the Army’s permit application, weather conditions at the time of

detonation not only affect the operational safety of the treatment activity itself but also the

anticipated environmental and human health effects that may result. Most significantly, both

       32.     The public notification, sampling, and cleanup requirements in EPA’s emergency

Background

In March 2026, the Army notified the EPA that 68 containers of unstable lead azide had been
discovered in two bunkers at the facility. At the time of the discovery, the lead azide was crystalizing, in
a dangerous and unstable condition, raising concerns that it could self-detonate. After further

To date, the Permittee has applied for, and the EPA has issued, three 90-day emergency permits for in-
place storage of the lead azide. The EPA has issued each succeeding permit prior to expiration of the
prior permit, with a legal notice published in the Hawk Eye newspaper announcing the issuance of the

Region 7 has maintained regular weekly calls with the Army’s personnel to encourage timely
development of the emergency permit application for treatment. The EPA has also sent numerous
letters to the Army outlining the expected contents of the application and requesting additional
information to ensure a complete application is submitted. Army’s October 2026 permit application
proposes a controlled treatment activity of the containers of waste lead azide by simultaneous
detonation. The containers will stay within the bunkers where explosive charges and an accelerant will
be placed on/next to each drum.

Legal Authority

This Emergency Permit is being issued upon the EPA’s finding of an imminent and substantial
endangerment to human health and the environment pursuant to the Solid Waste Disposal Act
(Sections 3004(a), (u), (v), and 3005 of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA (42 U.S.C.
§§ 6924(a), (u), (v); 6925)) and regulations promulgated thereunder (Title 40 of the Code of Federal
Regulations (C.F.R) Part 264, Subpart X; section 270.61). Pursuant to 40 C.F.R. § 270.61(a)(2), if the
Director (defined by regulation as the “the Regional Administrator . . . or an authorized
representative”) “finds an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health or the
environment the Director may issue a temporary emergency permit . . . to a permitted facility to allow
treatment, storage, or disposal of hazardous waste not covered by an effective permit.” The EPA issued
Army a RCRA permit in 2018 (“2018 RCRA Permit”), but that permit does not address this storage and
treatment location or proposed treatment method.

Conditions supporting issuance of an emergency permit pursuant to 40 C.F.R. § 270.61(a)(2) are
present. First, the lead azide in storage at IAAAP is a RCRA hazardous waste with waste codes D003
(reactivity) and D008 (toxicity characteristic for lead). Second, the storage location and off-site areas
that will be affected by intentional detonation of this waste are not covered by the 2018 RCRA Permit,
nor is this treatment method of lead azide authorized under that permit. Third, the current conditions
at IAAAP create an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment.
Due to deterioration during long-term storage, the lead azide is in an unstable, crystallizing state.
Crystal formation increases the probability of spontaneous detonation because the crystalized form of
lead azide is significantly more sensitive to shock and friction. With colder temperatures now
approaching in Iowa, the water-ethanol mixture that surrounds the cotton bags of lead azide in each
container would begin to cycle through freeze and thaw conditions, creating friction within the
containers. Importantly, the bunkers in which the waste is stored are not temperature controlled, and
although they were designed to mitigate blast impacts, they were not constructed to withstand an

Special Emergency Permit Conditions

The Permittee’s intentional detonation of lead azide will cause a significant release of lead into the
environment that presents numerous routes of potential human and ecological exposure. The
exposure risk presented by the treatment activity has both on- and off-site components. To make the
Emergency Permit optimally protective of human health and the environment, the EPA has
incorporated special permit conditions that are summarized in Attachment 3.

On-Site Impacts

Within IAAAP’s fenceline, the detonation is expected to result in contamination of soil, surface water,
sediment, and groundwater. Upon conducting the detonation, the Permittee is required to activate
and implement its Contingency Plan for Treatment to ensure worker safety. After the detonation, the
Permittee will implement the environmental monitoring program and the Closure Plan to characterize
and clean up detonation-related contamination on the IAAAP property. The Emergency Permit also
obligates the Permittee to utilize the step-out sampling protocols set forth in its Permit Application to
identify any contaminants that deposited in soils, groundwater, surface water and sediment beyond
the facility’s boundary. Due to IAAAP’s security restrictions, potential human exposure to detonation-
related contaminants surrounding the treatment area will be prevented during implementation of the
remedial activities.

In addition to treatment-related impacts within IAAAP, the detonation is expected to generate fine
lead-oxide particles that will become airborne, travel downwind at distance from the facility, and
deposit at ground-surface. This downwind dispersion and deposition of airborne lead presents
significant potential for human exposure. The Emergency Permit seeks to mitigate such risk through
permit conditions that: 1) require the Permittee to provide meaningful prior public notifications;
2) avoid detonation during defined adverse meteorological conditions and dates that would be likely to
impact densely populated downwind areas; and 3) obligate the Permittee to immediately sample and
remediate properties impacted by downwind deposition above a regulatory threshold.

Public Notifications

The first measure of protectiveness is prior public notification of risk posed to areas that will possibly
be impacted by airborne dispersion and deposition of lead resulting from the detonation. To
implement these notifications, the Emergency Permit obligates the Permittee to model depositional
impacts and airborne plume migration prior to any targeted detonation date using weather conditions
that are forecasted for the date/time of detonation. The modeling outputs must be updated and
publicly distributed at specific intervals before the targeted detonation date. The first public
notification must occur five days before detonation, followed by an updated notification two days
prior, and then hourly updates beginning 6 hours before the detonation is scheduled to occur. The
intent of such iterative modeling is to refine the predicted impact area based on more accurate
weather forecasting. This will provide the public with as much certainty as possible regarding expected
geographic impact of both deposition- and air-related impacts resulting from the detonation.

Importantly, the required modeling must utilize a conservative coding input to ensure that the
Permittee’s modeling does not under-predict the extent of potential impact. See Attachment 4.
Specifically, the modeling must be calculated using an Emission Factor of 1.00, which is a coding
parameter that assumes 100 percent of lead content will be released to the ambient air. Technical
experts from both the EPA and the Army agree that this is an overly conservative assumption and will
not be necessarily representative of actual conditions that result from the treatment activity. The EPA
acknowledges the Army’s real-world experience and expert judgment, presented in its permit
application, that the realistic airborne release of lead will, in fact, be less than 100 percent due to
considerable measures the Permittee will implement to mitigate blast effects. However, considering
technical uncertainty regarding a quantifiable reduction of the lead release produced by mitigation
measures, the EPA has chosen a conservative Emission Factor to ensure that the prior notifications are
maximally protective of the public.

notifications must communicate specific advisory messaging to aid and encourage people within

Meteorological Restrictions

The Emergency Permit’s second measure to optimize protectiveness is the identification of
meteorological conditions during which the treatment activity is not to occur. Weather conditions not
only affect the operational safety of the treatment activity but also the anticipated environmental and
human health effects that may result. Most significantly, both Army and EPA air dispersion modeling
indicates that wind speed and direction will have a direct influence on the path and scale of the
expected depositional and airborne impact areas.

To minimize the magnitude of human health risk, the Emergency Permit requires the Army to exercise
reasonable best efforts to avoid conducting the treatment activity if dust-lead deposition is predicted
to impact high-population-density areas to the east of the facility. These areas are defined by
U.S. Census Tracts that are individually correlated with population density data that is comparatively
higher than surrounding census tracts in Iowa and Illinois. Critically, census tracts provide a bright-line
boundary against which the Permittee can readily compare depositional modeling footprints, enabling
swift operational decision-making. Additionally, for the purpose of permit compliance, the EPA can use
this data to objectively validate the Permittee’s conduct of the treatment activity.

This directional constraint incorporates a geographic limitation to preserve sufficient operational
flexibility for the Permittee. Census Tract 7 of Des Moines County, Iowa, is omitted from the list of
designated census tracts to which depositional impact should be avoided. Exclusion of Census Tract 7

Permittee’s conscious avoidance of depositional impact to Census Tract 8 would guard against impact
to the most populated portion of Census Tract 7.

alternatives for the treatment of the lead azide in storage at IAAAP. In January 2026,
the Army activated an operational planning team (OPT) to explore potential treatment
alternatives. The OPT was tasked to develop an actionable plan that considered the
acute explosive hazard associated with this material and that could be executed in a
manner that ensured the safety of Army personnel and the surrounding community. An
initial assessment revealed complexities that required the involvement of additional
subject matter experts from across the U.S. Department of War, including the
Department of War Explosives Safety Office (DWESO). Personnel from other federal
agencies were also engaged, including the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and
Explosives (ATF) and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7; representatives
from both agencies regularly participated in OPT meetings throughout the process.

From January through April 2026, this multi-agency working group spent many hours
conducting extensive literature searches, technical evaluations, and risk analyses of the
full range of potential treatment alternatives. The OPT also performed blast effect
analysis, explosives safety quantity distance calculations using advanced modeling and
simulation, atmospheric plume modeling, and testing of specialized protective
engineering controls. During the development and evaluation of potential alternatives,
safety was identified as the single threshold criterion: a fundamental standard and
mandatory requirement that must be satisfied for a potential alternative to be considered
for selection and implementation.

The following broad categories of alternatives were considered: (1) in-situ chemical
treatment; (2) closed-chamber thermal treatment; (3) relocation of individual drums for

magazines.

The OPT evaluated a wide range of potential reagents for in-situ treatment. This
evaluation included the proprietary reagent MuniRem®, as well as sodium hydroxide,
potassium bichromate, sodium nitrite, glacial acetic acid, and ceric ammonium nitrate.
All methods of in-situ chemical treatment, regardless of reagent, require the drums to be
opened to initiate the treatment. Potential migration of lead azide crystals into the lid
rings and closure gaskets present an acute risk of unintentional detonation if an attempt
is made to open the drums. Opening the drums requires the application of rotational
torque that can create localized friction and shear forces that exceed the ignition
threshold of the lead azide. Furthermore, chemical treatment requires physical mixing
to achieve direct reagent-to-compound contact. Inserting mechanical impellers,
chemical sparge wands, ultrasonic agitation devices, or other tools into the drums can
introduce pinch points, cutting friction, and shear forces, resulting in risk of uncontrolled
detonation. As a result of these considerations, explosives safety experts from the
Army, DWESO, and ATF universally agreed that all alternatives involving in-situ
chemical treatment failed to meet the threshold criterion.

On- and off-site closed-chamber thermal treatment, in both an armored, fuel-fired
deactivation furnace and a rotary kiln incinerator, and relocation of individual drums for
treatment by open detonation were also evaluated. These methods of treatment require
manipulation and relocation of the drums, either by Army personnel or remotely
operated equipment. Physical lifting, tilting, rigging, or reorienting of the drums using
conventional forklifts or remote robotic systems generates internal movement, shifts the
drum contents, and introduces drop risk, all of which could spark rapid auto-ignition
resulting in unintentional detonation. Transporting the drums over interior floors, loading
aprons, conveyor rollers, or roadways exposes the contents to continuous vibrational
harmonics, transit shocks, and mechanical jolts. Under these conditions, an initiation in
a single drum would propagate instantly across adjacent containers, resulting in an
uncontrolled detonation. Based on these considerations, explosives safety experts from
the Army, DWESO, and ATF universally agreed that all alternatives requiring
manipulation or relocation of the drums do not meet the threshold criterion.

Following a series of briefings to increasingly higher leadership within the Army, the
Secretary of the Army selected in-place, controlled, intentional detonation for treatment
of the lead azide on May 8, 2026. This decision is supported by the technical
consensus across military and federal explosive safety authorities that this is the only

NOT SCHEDULED FOR ORAL ARGUMENT

              IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
                      FOR THE EIGHTH CIRCUIT



IOWA ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, et al.,

AGENCY, et al.,

RESPONDENTS’ NOTICE OF THE ARMY’S INTENT TO RESPOND TO
 IMMEDIATE THREAT UNDER RCRA’S EMERGENCY EXCLUSION

      The Government notifies the Court that the Department of the Army (“Army”)

intends to invoke the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to EPA’s

regulatory and permitting Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (“RCRA”)

requirements, under which the Army may perform treatment by controlled

detonation of the lead azide waste without the Emergency Permit that is challenged

in this petition. See 40 C.F.R. §§ 264.1(g)(8)(i)(D), 270.1(c)(3)(i)(D). There is an

immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (the

“Facility”) will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees

Fahrenheit in the next several days. The Army must perform a controlled detonation

                                         1
 to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion,

and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026. A controlled detonation allows

the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the

risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from

the Facility. The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency

Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation

measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled

detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion.

      The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is

therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s

administrative stay. But out of an abundance of caution, the Army provides this

notice to explain, for the Court’s benefit, the immediate threat of an imminent

explosion of lead azide at the Facility.

I.    The Army does not need a permit under EPA’s RCRA regulations to
      conduct a controlled detonation of the lead azide at the Facility in this
      emergency situation.

      There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Facility will

spontaneously explode. See Declaration of Col Aaron Teller. The waste has

deteriorated to a degree that it is extremely sensitive to friction from crystal

formation. Id. ¶ 9. The barrels holding the waste cannot be removed due to the risk

of explosion, which prevents the Army from taking other measures to reduce that


                                           2
 risk. Id. ¶¶ 12-13. As the outside temperatures drop the risk of an uncontrolled

explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing

temperatures. Id. ¶ 13. If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction

detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the

environment. Id. ¶ 15. Temperatures have already dropped below 30 degrees

Fahrenheit, with temperature swings as low as 24 degrees and high as 70 degrees.

Id. ¶¶ 28-29. These recent temperature swings have dramatically increased the risk

of an uncontrolled explosion and threat to public safety. Id. ¶ 29. Further, the

bunkers, where the barrels are located, are now more vulnerable to temperature

changes because the blast doors were removed in preparation of the controlled

detonation and cannot be replaced. Id. ¶ 27.

      Under these circumstances, EPA’s RCRA regulations provide an exemption

from both substantive and permitting requirements to allow immediate action. The

RCRA regulations provide that the substantive standards “do not apply to”:

      a person engaged in treatment or containment activities during
      immediate response to . . . [a]n immediate threat to human health,
      public safety, property, or the environment, from the known or
      suspected presence of military munitions, other explosive material, or
      an explosive device, as determined by an explosive or munitions
      emergency response specialist as defined in 40 C.F.R. § 260.10.

40 C.F.R. § 264.1(g)(8)(i)(D). The same exclusion from permitting requirements is

at 40 C.F.R. § 270.1(c)(3)(i)(D).



                                        3
       Here, an explosive or munitions emergency specialist has made the requisite

determination. Teller Decl. ¶ 3. Thus, EPA’s RCRA regulations allow the Army to

conduct a controlled detonation of the lead azide at the Facility even if the

Emergency Permit that is at issue in this case is not in effect. As will be addressed

further in the Government’s response to Petitioners’ stay motion that the

Government will file tomorrow, a controlled detonation is the safest way to prevent

an uncontrolled explosion of the lead azide. See Teller Declaration ¶¶ 18-25. Any

other options require handling the lead azide in a way that poses an unacceptable

risk of an uncontrolled explosion. Id. ¶¶ 6-17.

      A controlled detonation minimizes the risk associated with the resulting

explosion. Id. ¶¶ 16-25. During a controlled detonation, the Army can implement

a full suite of mitigation efforts including, providing advance public notice;

performing the detonation under favorable weather conditions (e.g., less wind, light

rain) to mitigate the spread of lead dust; wetting to reduce lead dust dispersal;

treating the lead to prevent only a partial detonation; facilitating any necessary

community evacuation; and monitoring to identify where any lead dust may spread

and where any environmental response actions may be needed. Id. ¶¶ 18-25. Indeed,

in preparation for the controlled detonation, the Army has already constructed

protective barriers around the munitions bunkers to minimize the escape of blast

material. Id. ¶ 21.


                                         4
       A spontaneous explosion, on the other hand, is much riskier. In an

uncontrolled explosion, the Army cannot implement its robust mitigation efforts.

Failing to treat all the lead azide, for example, could result in a random dispersal of

explosive material. Id. ¶ 17. This partially exploded lead azide could explode later

—a second spontaneous explosion—creating extremely unsafe conditions for the

public and for personnel conducting post-detonation cleanup. Id. Unfavorable winds

could increase the dispersion of lead dust in the community. Id. ¶ 25. And without

public notice, the public may panic upon the spontaneous explosion. A controlled

detonation is unquestionably much more protective to the public than an

uncontrolled explosion.

      A controlled detonation is necessary now to respond to the immediate threat

of an uncontrolled explosion of military munitions at the Facility. EPA’s regulations

allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit and the Army intends

to act on November 24, 2026.

II.   The administrative stay does not bar the Army’s emergency response.

      A stay and an injunction do different things. A stay “operates upon the

judicial proceeding itself” by “temporarily divesting an order of enforceability,”

while an injunction “is directed at someone, and governs that party’s conduct.” Nken

v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 428–29 (2009). The Court’s order stays EPA’s Emergency

Permit. It suspends the authority the Permit conferred, but it does not enjoin or


                                          5
 otherwise prohibit the Army from acting under a separate legal authority that does

not depend on the Emergency Permit. Because 40 C.F.R. § 264.1(g)(8)(i) and

§ 270.1(c)(3) of EPA’s regulations allow the Army’s planned action without a

permit, the stay does not reach it.

      RCRA’s emergency exclusion controls here. An uncontrolled detonation of

nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the

surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to

minimize the risks from the blast—harm that cannot be undone. Teller Decl. ¶¶ 16-

17. The environmental and health interests Petitioners seek to protect plainly are

better served by a controlled detonation than by an uncontrolled explosion, which

would not allow for wetting the blast material, control the timing to align with

favorable weather conditions, and prior public notification, and could scatter

partially destroyed lead azide. Id. ¶¶ 14–15, 17–21. The real choice, in other words,

is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated

detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion. To protect its personnel

and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action. Protection

of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.




                                         6
                                  CONCLUSION

      The Army intends to perform a controlled detonation of the lead azide at the

Facility by November 24, 2026, to protect the public from the more significant and

unacceptable threat of an uncontrolled explosion.

                                            Respectfully submitted,

ll. The IAAAP operating contractor, American Ordnance (AO), historically does

 which can increase sensitivity of the crystals and cause an uncontrolled detonation. Even a small

 lead azide explosive by directing blast effects downward and also enhance consumption of the

      Respondents United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) et al.

notify the Court of their intent to file a response on or before November 22, 2026, to

Petitioners’ emergency motion to stay an emergency permit that EPA issued to the

Department of the Army (“Army”) on November 13, 2026 (“Emergency Permit”).

The Emergency Permit authorized the Army to conduct a controlled detonation of

unstable and dangerous explosives – lead azide waste – upon EPA’s finding that the

waste and other attendant circumstances pose an imminent and substantial

endangerment to human health and the environment under the Resource

Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA).           See Emergency Hazardous Waste
                                          1

   Appellate Case: 26-3374    Page: 1    Date Filed: 11/20/2026 Entry ID: 5708407
 Management Facility Permit for Storage and Treatment of Lead Azide, EPA RCRA

ID No. IA7213820445 (Entry ID 5708024 at 6-31). On November 19, 2026,

Petitioners filed a petition review and an emergency motion to stay the Emergency

Permit. That same day, this Court administratively stayed the Emergency Permit

until the Court rules on Petitioners’ emergency motion.

      The Army had initially scheduled to detonate this lead azide waste at the Iowa

Army Ammunition Plant on November 20, 2026, in accordance with the terms of

the Emergency Permit. The Army thereafter delayed the planned detonation to

Monday, November 23, 2026. https://www.army.mil/article/296926. In a press

release announcing the postponement, the Army stated that “[t]his will delay the

detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop,

which would risk further destabilization of the material.”                 Moreover,

notwithstanding EPA’s issuance of the Emergency Permit, in qualifying emergency

situations, EPA’s RCRA regulations authorize the Army (which is not a party to this

petition for review) to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit

where it determines that there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety,

This Emergency Permit is required to protect human health and the environment and to authorize the

Emergency Permit, allow for the implementation of the treatment activity to safely manage the
explosive hazard. To maximize protection of public health, the Emergency Permit requires the

detonation date. The required modeling must utilize a conservative coding input to ensure that the

considerable measures the Permittee will implement to mitigate blast effects. However, considering
